---
title: "k-Nearest Neighbors Regression"
subtitle: "Total Phosphorus — a rise that levels into a plateau"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(caret)
source("R/utils.R")
non_linear_wq <- readr::read_csv("data/synthetic/non_linear_wq.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tp_wq <- non_linear_wq |> filter(analyte == "Total Phosphorus")
```

## Predicting by averaging nearby points

Total Phosphorus rises through the middle years of the record and then settles onto a plateau. That shape doesn't match the case studies covered so far: [piecewise regression](piecewise-regression.qmd) assumes a single slope break, [changepoint detection](changepoint-detection.qmd) assumes a single level shift, and neither describes a smooth rise into a plateau. There's also no single point an analyst could point to as "the" knot.

**k-nearest-neighbors (k-NN) regression** handles this by not committing to any functional form at all. For a query point $x_0$ on `year_frac`, it finds the $k$ training observations closest to it (Euclidean distance on `year_frac`) — call this neighborhood $N_k(x_0)$ — and predicts the plain average of their responses:

$$\hat y(x_0) = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i \in N_k(x_0)} y_i.$$

This is a lookup-and-average rule applied at prediction time, and it breaks from every method in this site so far in one specific way: those methods all still fit a linear predictor underneath, even when the shape looks nonlinear. [Piecewise regression](piecewise-regression.qmd)'s hinge term, for instance, is just an extra column handed to `lm()` — see [The Regression Framework](regression-framework.qmd) for why that still counts as "linear." k-NN has no linear predictor at all: no coefficients are estimated, just this neighborhood average, recomputed fresh at each query point.

Concentration data is modeled on the log scale throughout this site for the reasons covered in [Transformations](transformations.qmd) — a multiplicative process where variability scales with the mean — and Total Phosphorus is no exception; `log(result)` is used below.

## The shape in the record

```{r}
#| label: tp-raw-series
#| message: false
ggplot(tp_wq, aes(year_frac, result)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Total Phosphorus — raw scale", y = "Phosphorus (mg/L)") +
  nlt_theme
```

An early low, roughly flat stretch, a rise through the middle years, and a plateau at a higher level for the remainder of the record — the shape a logistic curve would produce, though nothing here assumes that form.

## Choosing k: the bias-variance tradeoff

$k$ is the one tuning parameter this method has, and it controls a direct bias-variance tradeoff. A small $k$ averages over only a handful of nearby points, so the fitted curve tracks the training data's noise as much as its signal — *low bias, high variance*. A large $k$ averages over a wide neighborhood, smoothing away real curvature along with the noise — *low variance, high bias*. There's no fitted coefficient to inspect here, so the tradeoff has to be shown, not asserted:

```{r}
#| label: tp-knn-sweep
#| message: false
grid <- data.frame(year_frac = seq(min(tp_wq$year_frac), max(tp_wq$year_frac), length.out = 300))

sweep_ks <- c(3, 20, 60)
sweep_fits <- lapply(sweep_ks, function(k) {
  m <- knnreg(log(result) ~ year_frac, data = tp_wq, k = k)
  grid |> mutate(fit = exp(predict(m, newdata = grid)), k = factor(k))
})
sweep_df <- bind_rows(sweep_fits)

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = tp_wq, aes(year_frac, result), alpha = 0.35, color = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = sweep_df, aes(year_frac, fit, color = k), linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Total Phosphorus — k-NN fit at three values of k", y = "Phosphorus (mg/L)", color = "k") +
  nlt_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

At $k = 3$ the curve is jagged, chasing individual points rather than the underlying rise; at $k = 60$ it's smoothed almost flat, blunting the plateau's onset; $k = 20$ sits between the two, tracking the rise without visibly reacting to single points.

Rather than pick a value by eye, $k$ is chosen by 10-fold cross-validation, minimizing mean squared error on the log scale across held-out folds:

```{r}
#| label: tp-knn-cv
set.seed(1)
folds <- createFolds(tp_wq$result, k = 10)
candidate_ks <- c(3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45, 60)

cv_mse <- sapply(candidate_ks, function(k) {
  fold_errs <- sapply(folds, function(idx) {
    train <- tp_wq[-idx, ]
    test <- tp_wq[idx, ]
    m <- knnreg(log(result) ~ year_frac, data = train, k = k)
    mean((log(test$result) - predict(m, newdata = test))^2)
  })
  mean(fold_errs)
})

data.frame(k = candidate_ks, cv_mse = round(cv_mse, 4))
```

```{r}
#| label: tp-knn-final
best_k <- candidate_ks[which.min(cv_mse)]
fit_tp <- knnreg(log(result) ~ year_frac, data = tp_wq, k = best_k)
best_k
```

Cross-validated error is minimized at $k =$ `r best_k`, consistent with the sweep above: small enough to track the rise-and-plateau shape, large enough that no single observation swings the prediction.

## The fitted curve

```{r}
#| label: tp-knn-fit-plot
grid <- grid |> mutate(fit = exp(predict(fit_tp, newdata = grid)))

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = tp_wq, aes(year_frac, result), alpha = 0.4, color = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(year_frac, fit), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Total Phosphorus — k-NN fit (k = %d)", best_k), y = "Phosphorus (mg/L)") +
  nlt_theme
```

No confidence band is shown here, because none is available: `knnreg()` produces a fitted value at each point, without a coefficient or a standard error behind it. That rules out a significance test, a slope estimate, or a p-value. This fit is best read as a **prediction-oriented baseline**: the cross-validated MSE above (`r round(min(cv_mse), 4)` on the log scale) is the one number the method offers, and it measures how well the rule predicts held-out points, not whether the apparent trend is statistically real.

## Interpretation

k-NN recovers the rise-and-plateau shape using only a neighborhood-averaging rule tuned by cross-validation, without being told any functional form. That makes it useful for showing what the record looks like, and nothing more: no coefficient says how fast Phosphorus rose, no interval bounds where the plateau sits, and no test distinguishes a real leveling-off from a stretch where the data happens to thin out. The next section fits [LOESS](loess-smoothing.qmd) to the same data. LOESS replaces k-NN's local average with a locally weighted regression — still no global functional form, but a step closer to the kind of fit a formal model can be built on.

## Extending this analysis

A rise-then-plateau shape like this one is exactly what a logistic growth curve describes, and k-NN's fitted curve gives a reasonable read of that shape from the raw data alone. If that read holds up, fitting the logistic form directly with `nls()` can serve this specific shape better than the fully nonparametric route this site takes through LOESS and a GAM. A logistic fit recovers a rate parameter, an inflection point, and confidence intervals on both — inferential machinery k-NN structurally can't provide — using far fewer parameters than a smooth-basis fit needs. This is a genuine tradeoff against the GAM route taken here, and it comes with its own cost: a parametric curve fit this way is only as good as the assumption that the shape really is logistic, an assumption the GAM never has to make.
